draft.title: Empirical formulas and percentage composition
card: Empirical formula
the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound. For example, CH₂O is the empirical formula of a compound whose formula could be C₂H₄O₂.
Finding it
Divide each element's mass by its molar mass to get moles. Divide every answer by the smallest one. If the results are not whole numbers, multiply them all by the same small number until they are.
Percentage composition
the mass of an element in a compound as a percentage of the compound's total mass. % of element = mass of element ÷ mass of compound × 100.
Percentages can be used as if they were masses out of 100 g. This lets you find an empirical formula from percentage data.
draft.remember: Masses become moles, moles become the simplest ratio, and that ratio is the empirical formula.

a.q: A compound contains 1.2 g of carbon and 0.2 g of hydrogen only. What is its empirical formula? (C = 12, H = 1.0 g/mol)
a.why: Carbon is 1.2 ÷ 12 = 0.10 mol and hydrogen is 0.2 ÷ 1.0 = 0.20 mol. The ratio is 1 : 2, so the formula is CH₂. CH comes from comparing masses rather than moles.
a.clue: Change each mass to moles before comparing.

b.q: A sample of an oxide of nitrogen is 63.7% nitrogen and 36.3% oxygen by mass. What is its empirical formula? (N = 14.0, O = 16.0 g/mol)
b.why: In 100 g there are 63.7 ÷ 14.0 = 4.55 mol of N and 36.3 ÷ 16.0 = 2.27 mol of O. Dividing by 2.27 gives a ratio of 2 : 1, so the formula is N₂O. NO is tempting only if the percentages are compared directly instead of as moles.
b.clue: Treat the percentages as grams in a 100 g sample.

problems.detail: Why (a) says CH comes from comparing masses rather than moles. Comparing the masses 1.2 : 0.2 gives 6 : 1, which is C₆H, not CH. The distractor is misattributed, and students who check it will be confused.

Why (b) says NO is tempting 'only' if the percentages are compared directly. Comparing 63.7 : 36.3 directly gives about 1.75 : 1, not 1 : 1, so this explanation of the NO distractor does not hold. The absolute 'only' is also unsupported.

check.summary: Both questions have correct intended answers (CH₂ and N₂O), and the card is accurate. The explanations misdescribe the distractors: comparing masses in (a) gives C₆H, not CH, and comparing percentages directly in (b) does not give NO.
